deep.reconstruction:
Problem: find the locus of the apex C of all spherical triangles on a fixed base AB with fixed area, i.e. fixed spherical excess E.

Construction (Gauss): take one such triangle ABC. Let M and N be the midpoints of AC and BC, and draw the great circle g through M and N. Through C draw the small circle parallel to g, meaning the curve of points at the same spherical distance h from g as C. Gauss claims this small circle is the locus.

Proof sketched by the figure (the details are made explicit here, my wording): drop perpendicular arcs from A, B, C to g, with feet A', B', C'.
- Triangles A A' M and C C' M are congruent: right angles at A' and C', vertical angles at M, and equal hypotenuses MA = MC. Hence AA' = CC'.
- In the same way, triangles B B' N and C C' N are congruent, so BB' = CC' = h.
- CC' splits the part of the triangle above g into the two pieces labelled '1'. These are congruent to the pieces cut off at A and B below g.
- By cut-and-paste, area(ABC) equals the area of the quadrilateral A B B' A' (the pieces 1+2+3+4). This quadrilateral has right angles at A' and B' and equal legs AA' = BB' = h, i.e. it is a spherical Saccheri quadrilateral.

Why the locus works (also implicit, my wording): let C* be any point at distance h from g on the side opposite A and B.
- The arc AC* meets g at a point P. The right triangles A A' P and C* C*' P have equal legs and vertical angles at P, so they are congruent and P is the midpoint of AC*.
- Likewise the midpoint of BC* lies on g. So for every C* the midpoint great circle is the same g.
- The quadrilateral ABB'A' is determined by AB and g alone, so area(ABC*) = area(ABC).

The 'parallel small circle' passes through the antipodes of A and B, since the antipode of A lies at distance h from g on the opposite side. So it is exactly Lexell's circle. The faint pencil note 'Zweiter Fall' probably refers to the configuration where the perpendicular feet fall outside the segments (or to the mirror locus on the other side of AB).

In coordinates (mine): take g as the equator, A = (cos h cos q, -cos h sin q, sin h), B = (cos h cos q, cos h sin q, sin h), C = (cos h cos t, cos h sin t, -sin h). Then tan(E/2) = |A·(B×C)|/(1+A·B+B·C+C·A) = sin h·tan q, which is independent of t.
errors: No real error. The argument tacitly assumes a configuration in which the feet of the perpendiculars lie as drawn and the triangle is 'small'. Other configurations need a signed-area version, and the pencil 'Zweiter Fall' suggests Gauss knew a second case must be treated.

The page does not state that the locus consists of two arcs, or that it is only the arc of the small circle on the far side of AB from g. Points of the small circle on the other side of the line through A and B give the complementary/negative orientation.

results.what: Locus of the apex of spherical triangles with given base and given area is a small circle (through the antipodes of A, B), parallel to the great circle through the midpoints of the two lateral sides.
results.usually_credited_to: A. J. Lexell (1781, publ. 1784); also treated by Euler (1778/1797)

results.what: Proof by midpoint great circle and dropped perpendiculars: congruent right triangles reduce the triangle to a Saccheri quadrilateral on AB independent of C.
results.modern_name: Midline / Saccheri-quadrilateral proof of Lexell's theorem (standard textbook proof, also used for area in neutral geometry)
results.usually_credited_to: Commonly associated with Steiner (1827) and later textbook treatments; Legendre-type equivalence proofs

deep.surprise_reason: Lexell's theorem was published two to three decades earlier. Gauss's synthetic cut-and-paste proof is elegant and predates Steiner's 1827 treatment if the 1809 dating holds, but it is a known style of proof and the result is not his. It is a notable but minor private note.

checkable.asserts: tan(E/2) of triangle ABC equals -sin(h)*tan(q) (sign is orientation), independent of t: the area is constant on the small circle z=-sin h
The midpoints of AC and BC lie on the great circle z=0 for every C on the parallel circle (with A, B, C as above)
The antipode of A lies on the locus circle z=-sin h, so the circle is Lexell's circle through the antipodes A*, B*

transcription_corrections: The figure label near B appears to read '1+4' (or similar) rather than a separate '4'; the regions are 1,1 at C, 2,2, 3, 4 and '1+4'.
'[-aller-]' is struck through; the visible deleted word may be 'aller' or 'der'. The reading 'der Spitze ... sphaerischen Dreiecke' stands.
'gegebenen Inhalte' should be read as 'gegebenem Inhalte' (dative), as written by Gauss.
